claims.text: The initial material is a single-phase FCC alloy containing 3d transition metals and non-magnetic elements.
Replacing 10% of Co with Fe is the controlled compositional intervention.
Co-to-Fe substitution will produce a heterogeneous microstructure containing ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic phases.
A balanced mixture of ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic interactions increases magnetic entropy change.
The balanced magnetic interactions produce a larger change in magnetization at low applied fields.
The larger low-field magnetization change enhances the magnetocaloric response.
The intervention will increase magnetocaloric entropy change by 20% relative to the baseline.
The intervention will decrease hysteresis loss by 15% relative to the baseline.
The intervention will increase yield strength by 10% relative to the baseline.
Rapid heat exchange will be maintained after compositional tuning.
The proposed relationships hold from 250 to 350 K at applied magnetic fields no greater than 2 T.
The proposed relationships are limited to rare-earth-free FCC high-entropy alloys containing mixtures of 3d transition metals and non-magnetic elements.
Failure to obtain at least a 15% increase in magnetocaloric response, a 10% decrease in hysteresis loss, or a 5% increase in yield strength will falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The baseline is described as 100% Co with no Fe, which is neither a multicomponent high-entropy alloy nor the stated mixture of 3d transition metals and non-magnetic elements.

The initial and bounded system is described as single-phase FCC, while the mediator invokes distinct ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic phases. Magnetic regions could coexist within one crystallographic phase, but the wording asserts a multiphase heterogeneous microstructure without reconciling it with the single-phase specification.
